headline: A short video game may spot depression

sources.title: Depression screening using video games (NIH Research Matters)
3-Minute Video Game Identifies Patients Who Have Depression (NYU Langone)
This 3-Minute Video Game Is Surprisingly Good at Spotting Depression (Gizmodo)

chunks.text: A short video game on a phone may help doctors spot [[depression]] in about three minutes. The illness is hard to [[measure]], so a team at New York University had to {{come up with}} a [[fresh]] way to test for it: two simple games. The team {{carried out}} a study where 120 people played the games, 50 with the illness and 70 without. The results were published in May in a major science [[journal]], and this month the National Institutes of Health [[featured]] the study in its health news for the public. One day, doctors could use short games like these [[instead of]] long [[questionnaires]].

verbs.correct: To invent a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To copy an older way of testing
verbs.why: A team can come up with a clever name for a new product, and engineers sometimes come up with a cheaper way to build something. A team at New York University came up with two short games to test for depression in just minutes.

verbs.correct: To do a piece of planned work
verbs.wrong: To pay for a piece of research
verbs.why: A hospital carries out safety checks every month, and a scientist carries out an experiment step by step. The NYU team carried out a study where 120 people played the games, 50 of them living with depression.

chunks.text: The first game asks players to pick apples from a tree on the screen. Every pick gives fewer apples, so each tree slowly {{runs low}} on fruit, and the player must decide when to {{move on}} to a fresh tree. [[On average]], healthy players {{held out}} until a tree was almost empty. Players with depression {{walked away from}} their trees much sooner, and the worse their illness was, the earlier they left. The game measures the moment when picking apples stops feeling [[rewarding]]. About 70 percent of people with depression lose [[pleasure]] in things they [[used to]] enjoy.

verbs.correct: To have less and less left
verbs.why: A printer can run low on ink in the middle of a big job, and water sometimes runs low on the third day of a hike. In the game's first task, each apple tree slowly runs low on fruit the longer a player keeps picking.

verbs.correct: To leave and go to the next thing
verbs.why: After years in one job, a person might feel ready to move on, and a meeting moves on to the next topic once everyone has spoken. In the apple game, the player must decide the exact moment to move on to a fresh tree.

verbs.correct: To continue for as long as possible
verbs.wrong: To count the apples one by one
verbs.why: A phone battery can hold out until the end of a long flight, and packed food might hold out for a whole camping trip. In the study, healthy players on average held out picking apples until a tree was almost empty.

verbs.correct: To leave something without finishing it
verbs.wrong: To shake something to get more fruit
verbs.why: Some people walk away from a well paid job to try something new, and you cannot always walk away from a project halfway through. In the study, players with depression walked away from their apple trees much sooner than healthy players did.

chunks.text: In the second game, players looked at 30 [[snacks]] and said what each one should cost. Then the game showed some players only the cheapest items, [[over and over]]. Healthy players changed their minds: seeing cheap snacks {{brought down}} the price they expected to pay, [[little by little]]. Players with depression mostly {{stuck with}} their first numbers. The scientists say their [[expectations]] did not [[adjust]] to the new situation, and that this stuck feeling may be an important part of the illness.

verbs.why: A new factory can bring down the price of batteries over time, and fresh competition often brings down airline fares. In the snack game, seeing cheap items again and again slowly brought down the price healthy players expected to pay.

verbs.correct: To keep using the same thing
verbs.why: Some people stick with the same hairdresser for twenty years, and a runner might stick with water instead of anything sweet during a race. In the snack game, players with depression mostly stuck with their first price guesses, even after seeing new information.

chunks.text: The team hopes to {{roll out}} the game to [[clinics]] one day and plans to ask US [[regulators]] for official [[approval]] as a medical [[device]]. Patients could also play at home once a week, so doctors can {{keep track of}} how well a [[treatment]] is working [[within]] two or three weeks instead of months. The researchers are careful about the [[limits]]. Not everyone with depression plays the same way, and a game cannot {{rule out}} that a player is simply tired or stressed. [[For now]], the game's job is to {{back up}} a doctor's opinion with extra information, not to [[replace]] the doctor.

verbs.wrong: To keep something secret for a time
verbs.why: A bank might roll out a new app in the spring, and a city can roll out electric buses one route at a time. The NYU team hopes to roll out its short game to clinics once it earns official approval.

Some people keep track of their spending in a small notebook, and a running app can keep track of how far you go each day. With this game, doctors could keep track of a patient's progress in a few weeks instead of months.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not possible
verbs.why: Doctors rule out a broken bone with a quick scan, and police sometimes cannot rule out any suspects early in a case. This game cannot rule out that a low score simply means a player is tired or stressed that day.

Two witnesses might back up a friend's story, and solid data can back up a coach's tough decision. For now, this game's job is to back up a doctor's opinion with extra information, not to replace the doctor.

mainIdea.s: Researchers built a short phone game that may show who has depression. Players with the illness left apple trees sooner and did not adjust their expectations.
mainIdea.why: The team carried out a study with 120 people. Depression showed in how soon players left trees and how little their expectations adjusted.

mainIdea.s: A quick phone game may help doctors find depression. In the study, people with the illness stayed at trees longer and changed prices faster than healthy players.
mainIdea.why: Close, but it is backwards. Players with depression left their trees sooner and mostly kept their first prices.

mainIdea.s: New York scientists released a free game that teaches students about mental health in their classes. Thousands of teenagers played it at school this past spring.
mainIdea.why: The article is about a three minute test that may spot depression, not a school game that teaches teenagers about mental health.

tf.s: The team carried out a study with 120 people, and 50 of them had depression
tf.why: The study included 120 people: 50 with depression and 70 without.

tf.s: Healthy players walked away from their trees sooner than players with depression

tf.s: The whole test takes about three minutes on a phone
tf.why: The article says the game takes about three minutes on a phone.
